newsitem.title: USA: Conoco seeks to keep Utah monument oil lease alive.
newsitem.headline: Conoco seeks to keep Utah monument oil lease alive.

text.p: DuPont Co subsidiary Conoco Inc said Wednesday it had filed an application to drill for oil on a lease it held in Utah to test how the government would handle land that President Bill Clinton set aside last year as a national monument.
Conoco Tuesday applied to drill on a state lease and a federal lease in the Reese Canyon area of the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.
When Clinton created the monument, calling it "some of the most remarkable land in the world," he said valid existing leases would be honored.
"What we really want to do is drill an exploratory well on the state lease," said Conoco spokesman Tom DeCola.
The company estimates that the area could hold more than a hundred million barrels of oil reserves. It has been considering drilling on the property over the last two years.

Conoco applied to drill on the federal lease in order to see whether the Interior Department's Bureau of Land Management would suspend the 10-year lease, which was due to expire in November. If the company failed to start drilling on the lease before the 10 years ran out, it would lose it, unless the clock was stopped by suspending the lease.

DeCola said Conoco had been willing to discuss suspending the lease without applying for a drilling permit, but Interior Department officials had said the company would have to apply for a permit first.
Grand Staircase-Escalante Monument manager Jerry Meredith said it was not unusual for a company to apply to drill on a lease just before it expired.
"I would have been surprised if they hadn't done something," Meredith said, explaining that when a company applies to drill, it can request that the clock on the lease be suspended.

In a February 11 letter, Interior Department Deputy Chief of Staff Susan Rieff told Conoco that the government would have to study the environmental impact of potential drilling before approving any permits.

Rieff said the environmental study process "could take some time, given the lack of development in the area and the need to measure the proposal against the historic and scientific values protected by the Monument designation."

If the study time approached the end of the term on the lease, "the Department would consider suspending the lease term to avoid lease expiration," the letter said, adding there was no guarantee the lease would be suspended.
DeCola said the company had waited until now to apply to drill in the area because technological advances had made it more promising only in the last few years.
"An area can become highly prospective simply because we have better tools evaluate it," he said.
